> less than one call in 100,000 across our evaluation runs

It's not that surprising, given that these models generate each new token by sampling from a context-determined probability distribution.

If you run the same prompt repeatedly many times, it becomes increasingly probable that a tiny percent of the generated sequences will go off in, ahem, unusual directions.

50250081.text:
Also, a word to the wise:

The reality of running recent Chinese open weight models is that they are all overtuned for successfully completing tasks. I can ask Qwen3.8 Flash Next to grep for regexes that use PHP-specific features that might be problematic to port to Rust. But instead of just grepping, Qwen3.8 FN will spend 30,000 tokens writing a Rust test harness, exhaustively check every regex, consult a bunch of docs, and write me a 2 page report. Q3.8 FN is deeply convinced that it's going to get extra credit for doing more than it is asked. (To be fair, it's a prototype release.)

But if your sandboxing isn't set up to handle some whacky weirdness, then you can't even trust Claude or ChatGPT. Which is important—the big vendors often do provide sandboxing or command filtering in their harnesses, but some popular local harnesses like Pi.dev are intended to rely on external sandboxing tools.

50250094.text:

Git commit hooks, python pth files, AGENTS.mds, subtle flaws in firewall rulesets, tweaked RNG code, the pseudorandom variance in it's token choice encoding a low bit rate message about where the defect is, or about what nice things it has found.

We're seeing the full court press of sockpuppet and bot accounts to downplay it, to confuse with unrelated topics like alignment and training data, to imply that using any model is the same as using an untrustworthy one.

No single model can be trusted, but especially not when it's masters have misalignment with your continued democracy, security or individual liberty. Think about that when you run Qwen or get cheap inference from Grok or Kimi.
